ocar.opportunity: A complete synaptic-resolution connectome supplies a substrate for hypotheses about circuits and cell identities. For years only C. elegans had such a map; a second, phylogenetically distant species of similar numerical complexity lets those hypotheses be tested in a chordate.
ocar.challenge: Ciona intestinalis is often treated as a chordate C. elegans, but it is a urochordate sibling of vertebrates, not an ecdysozoan. Homologies cannot be cherry-picked, and many larval neurons look idiosyncratic rather than like simplified vertebrate cells.
ocar.action: Ryan and Meinertzhagen, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (published 2019; DOI 2018), review EM reconstructions of the tadpole-larva central and peripheral nervous systems of Ciona intestinalis and the neuron types those maps define.
ocar.resolution: About 330 CNS cells are mostly ciliated ependymal cells, with ~180 neurons in about 50 morphological types. Most neurons are ciliated and lack dendrites; some lack an axon. Synapses are mostly en passant, some dyads, with heterogeneous vesicles, averaging 49 synapses per neuron, forming a network of unpredicted complexity.
ocar.future_work: Priorities named in the conclusions are whether a second larva would show identical types, cell-by-cell transmitters and receptors (single-cell transcriptomics were underway), and resisting the assumption that tunicate neurons are simply miniature vertebrate homologs.

summaries.beginner: A tiny sea-squirt larva has a complete wiring diagram of its small nervous system. This review catalogs the cell types in that map and warns that they are not just miniature vertebrate neurons.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019 version of a 2018 paper), Ryan and Meinertzhagen review EM connectomes of the Ciona intestinalis tadpole larva. The CNS has about 330 cells, mostly ciliated ependymal cells, and ~180 neurons in about 50 morphological types, with mixed chordate and idiosyncratic features. Synapses are largely en passant between axons and average 49 per neuron. The authors treat the maps as a second complete connectome after C. elegans, while emphasizing Ciona’s position as a vertebrate sibling rather than a nematode analog.
summaries.advanced: Counts (~330 CNS cells, ~180 neurons, ~50 types, 49 synapses/neuron) are those stated in the abstract and should be checked against the source reconstructions (Ryan et al.). This is a review of existing EM connectomes, not a new volume. The extract’s conclusions flag untested identity of types across larvae and incomplete transmitter assignments. PMC copy is an author manuscript.

plain_language_summary: A tiny sea-squirt larva has a complete wiring diagram of its small nervous system. This review catalogs the cell types in that map and warns that they are not just miniature vertebrate neurons.

ocar.opportunity: Connectome mapping has mostly treated connections as stable once formed. If local circuitry rewires during learning, the physical graph is a moving target and a possible therapeutic handle.
ocar.challenge: Evidence for rewiring has been hard to obtain, and structural change must be disentangled from synaptic-strength and excitability plasticity. Long-range tracts are unlikely to rewire extensively in the healthy adult brain.
ocar.action: Bennett, Kirby, and Finnerty, in Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews (2018), review evidence for rewiring at synaptic, microcircuit, and long-range scales and its role in learning.
ocar.resolution: They conclude there is growing evidence that the micro- and meso-connectome rewire during experience-dependent plasticity and learning, whereas long-range rewiring in healthy adults is limited to terminal arbours of projecting axons. Rewiring is argued to be especially useful where connection probability is already low, as among neocortical pyramids.
ocar.future_work: The authors list open questions on how rewiring affects function, how it is coordinated with other plasticity mechanisms, and how to control it therapeutically without causing aberrant wiring in psychiatric or neurological disease.

summaries.beginner: Brain maps often assume the wires stay put after they form. This review argues that local circuits do rewire during learning, which could matter for treating brain disease.
summaries.intermediate: Bennett, Kirby, and Finnerty (Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews, 2018) survey evidence that mammalian connectivity is not fixed. They examine rewiring from synapses and microcircuits up to long-range tracts, and they conclude that local circuitry rewires during learning while long-range axons in healthy adults mainly remodel terminal arbours. They argue that forming and losing entire connections expands learning capacity in sparsely connected cortex, and they discuss therapeutic use after injury and in neuropsychiatric disorders.
summaries.advanced: This is a narrative review, not a new reconstruction or a single experiment. The extract’s conclusion distinguishes micro/meso rewiring from limited long-range change but does not quantify rates. Disease-treatment claims are prospective. The supplied PDF is a King’s College accepted manuscript with publisher front matter.

plain_language_summary: Brain maps often assume the wires stay put after they form. This review argues that local circuits do rewire during learning, which could matter for treating brain disease.

ocar.opportunity: Fine-scale synaptic maps of identified cell classes can show whether excitatory and inhibitory neurons obey the same spatial wiring rules when they share a presynaptic pathway.
ocar.challenge: Peters’ rule predicts synapses from axonal–dendritic overlap, but prior work showed structured CA3–CA1 pyramidal connectivity, leaving open whether CA1 interneurons follow the same pattern.
ocar.action: Kwon, Feng, Druckmann, and Kim, in Journal of Neuroscience (2018), use mGRASP and neuTube in male mice to map Schaffer-collateral synapses onto CA1 pyramidal cells and parvalbumin-positive interneurons.
ocar.resolution: Pyramidal connectivity strongly departed from randomness, and applying Peters’ rule enhanced that structure, whereas PV cells were more random and became more so under Peters’ rule. Deep-versus-superficial sublayer structure was present for pyramids and little or none for PVs. The same SC axons therefore follow different rules onto the two targets.
ocar.future_work: The discussion links structured pyramidal input to branch-level nonlinear processing and more random PV input to broad winner-take-all inhibition; those functional interpretations are hypotheses for physiology, not tested here.

summaries.beginner: The same incoming axons in mouse hippocampus wire onto excitatory and inhibitory cells in different ways. Excitatory cells get a patterned map; a major inhibitory class looks more random.
summaries.intermediate: Kwon, Feng, Druckmann, and Kim (Journal of Neuroscience, 2018) map Schaffer-collateral synapses in male-mouse CA1 with mGRASP. CA3–CA1 pyramidal connectivity is spatially structured and becomes more so when overlap (Peters’ rule) is used to predict synapses, whereas parvalbumin-positive interneurons are closer to random and become more random under the same prediction. Deep pyramidal sublayer cells appear more structured than superficial ones; PVs show little sublayer specificity. The paper treats these as distinct connectivity rules for E versus I cells sharing one input stream.
summaries.advanced: Animals are male mice; PV cells are the only inhibitory class mapped. ‘Random’ is relative to spatial structure and Peters’ rule, not a claim of unstructured biology. Numeric R² values appear in figures rather than as a single summary statistic in the extract. Functional arguments about winner-take-all are interpretive.

plain_language_summary: The same incoming axons in mouse hippocampus wire onto excitatory and inhibitory cells in different ways. Excitatory cells get a patterned map; a major inhibitory class looks more random.

ocar.opportunity: Large-scale connectome projects treat whole-brain wiring diagrams as a genome-like resource. The only complete animal connectome for decades was already in hand: C. elegans.
ocar.challenge: Unlike the genetic code, there is no comparable theory that reads function off connectivity, so even a 302-neuron map has not yielded a complete account of behavior.
ocar.action: Schafer, in Trends in Neurosciences (2018), retells the White et al. (1986) reconstruction and its later influence on behavioral neuroscience and network science.
ocar.resolution: White and colleagues mapped 302 identified hermaphrodite neurons connected by approximately 10,000 chemical synapses and 1,000 gap junctions, by hand, from serial TEM. Schafer argues this diagram remains a guide to what connectomics can and cannot deliver as fly and mouse maps arrive.
ocar.future_work: The piece closes by calling for theories that relate network topology to circuit function, with C. elegans as the place to develop and test them before interpreting larger connectomes.

summaries.beginner: The first complete animal wiring diagram was the worm, finished in 1986 by hand. This essay says that map still teaches both the power and the limits of connectomics.
summaries.intermediate: In Trends in Neurosciences (2018), Schafer reviews the C. elegans connectome of White et al. (1986): 302 hermaphrodite neurons, about 10,000 chemical synapses and 1,000 gap junctions, reconstructed by serial TEM without modern volume-EM or tracing software. The male connectome is noted as a later addition. More than 30 years on, behavior is still incompletely explained from the graph, which Schafer contrasts with the genome’s genetic code. The essay is a historical and conceptual guide rather than a new reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: Synapse counts are those stated in this review (approximately 10,000 chemical, 1,000 electrical) and should be checked against later reannotations. ‘Only complete neuronal connectome’ is the 2018 claim; it is historically framed. The extract notes FIB-SEM and computer-assisted tracing as subsequent tools, not methods of the original map.

plain_language_summary: The first complete animal wiring diagram was the worm, finished in 1986 by hand. This essay says that map still teaches both the power and the limits of connectomics.

ocar.opportunity: Whether vertebrate motoneurons are recruited mainly by their biophysics or by specific interneuron-to-motoneuron wiring can be settled only with a complete local connection map.
ocar.challenge: It is controversial how much orderly recruitment depends on intrinsic differences among motoneurons versus selective presynaptic targeting.
ocar.action: Svara, Kornfeld, Denk, and Bollmann, in Cell Reports (2018), as described in the catalog abstract, map all connections from two interneuron types onto all motoneurons in a larval zebrafish spinal-cord hemisegment using serial block-face EM.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports specific connectivity from dorsal but not ventral excitatory ipsilateral interneurons onto large motoneurons used in strong force, matching dorsally located interneurons active only during fast swims. Inhibitory commissural-to-motoneuron connectivity lacked a discernible pattern. The wiring is taken as consistent with recruitment that depends to a considerable extent on specific connectivity.
ocar.future_work: How this hemisegment pattern generalizes along the cord and to other speeds is outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Fish swim by turning on bigger motor cells as they go faster. This study maps every local wire onto those cells in a stretch of larval zebrafish spinal cord and finds that some interneurons pick their motor targets on purpose.
summaries.intermediate: Svara, Kornfeld, Denk, and Bollmann (Cell Reports, 2018) use serial block-face EM to reconstruct connections from two interneuron classes onto all motoneurons in a larval zebrafish spinal hemisegment. According to the catalog abstract, dorsal excitatory ipsilateral interneurons synapse specifically onto large, high-force motoneurons, whereas ventral excitatory ipsilateral cells and inhibitory commissural cells do not show that specificity. The authors interpret the pattern as evidence that recruitment is not only a biophysical size principle. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Call et al., Nature (2026), on flexible oligodendrocyte ensheathment and paranodal bridges in zebrafish, mouse, and human, not the Svara et al. spinal connectome. Numbers and claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Cell Reports paper is required for methods, completeness, and figures.

plain_language_summary: Fish swim by turning on bigger motor cells as they go faster. This study maps every local wire onto those cells in a stretch of larval zebrafish spinal cord and finds that some interneurons pick their motor targets on purpose.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic partner choice can be separated from mere spatial adjacency only if both synapses and the 3D occupancy of processes are known in the same volume.
ocar.challenge: Peters’ rule and related spatial models may not explain why homologous C. elegans neurons make reproducible synapses despite variable process placement.
ocar.action: Brittin, Cook, Hall, Emmons, and Cohen, on bioRxiv (2018), volumetrically reconstruct the C. elegans nerve ring from legacy serial-section EM at L4 and young adult and compare spatial, synaptic, and subcellular specificity.
ocar.resolution: Neuron classes occupy defined neighborhoods and aggregate functionally similar synapses. Variability in process placement accounts for less than 20% of variability in synaptic connectivity, and spatial models cannot explain homologous-neuron reproducibility. A combinatorial cell-adhesion model still needed extra ingredients such as subcellular domains or alternative splicing to match observed specificity.
ocar.future_work: The authors conjecture a spatially constrained genetic model but show that cell-level combinatorial expression is insufficient without further specificity mechanisms.

summaries.beginner: In the worm’s nerve ring, being next to another cell is not enough to predict a synapse. This preprint rebuilds the 3D shapes of those processes at two ages and finds extra, non-spatial rules are needed.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2018), Brittin and colleagues volumetrically reconstruct the C. elegans nerve ring from legacy serial EM at L4 and young adult. They describe three layers of wiring specificity—spatial, synaptic, and subcellular—and report that process-placement variability accounts for less than 20% of synaptic-connectivity variability. Spatial-only models fail to capture reproducible synapses among homologous neurons. A combinatorial cell-adhesion-molecule model still required subcellular domains or alternative splicing to approach the observed specificity.
summaries.advanced: This is a 2018 preprint, not a journal version. The <20% figure is the authors’ stated partition of variability. Connectivity-fraction values cited from other systems (less than 0.25) are background, not new measurements here. Supplement examples (LUS scores) should not be treated as main-text summary statistics. Polyadic synapses are discussed as a further complication for genetic labeling models.

plain_language_summary: In the worm’s nerve ring, being next to another cell is not enough to predict a synapse. This preprint rebuilds the 3D shapes of those processes at two ages and finds extra, non-spatial rules are needed.

ocar.opportunity: The outer retina has stereotyped anatomical motifs at the photoreceptor synapse, so a complete 3D EM census can test whether those motifs are as strict as textbooks imply.
ocar.challenge: Classical EM and immunolabelling traded sample size against resolution, limiting quantitative connectivity to a few cells; a published mouse volume also lacked explicit synaptic labels.
ocar.action: Rogerson, Behrens, Euler, Berens, and Schubert, in Journal of Physiology (2017), review a 3D serial-EM analysis of mouse outer retina that infers contacts from invaginating versus basal motifs.
ocar.resolution: The quantitative description recovered unexpected exceptions: substantial rod–cone pathway interaction at the photoreceptor synapse, sparse photoreceptor sampling, and atypical contacts, including many rod-to-OFF cone-bipolar contacts. Rod-to-ON cone-bipolar contacts suggested elsewhere were not confirmed.
ocar.future_work: The functional weight of atypical contacts remains unsettled, given conflicting physiology, and the unlabeled-synapse inference is a standing limit of the source dataset.

summaries.beginner: Rod and cone pathways in the eye were thought to meet later in the circuit. This review of a 3D electron-microscope map of mouse outer retina finds they already mix at the first synapse, with several exceptions to the textbook wiring.
summaries.intermediate: Rogerson, Behrens, Euler, Berens, and Schubert (Journal of Physiology, 2017) review connectomic lessons from the outer retina, drawing on a mouse 3D serial-EM volume that lacks synaptic labels and therefore uses anatomical motifs to infer contacts. They highlight exceptions to classical ON-invaginating and OFF-basal sampling of all cones in a dendritic span, including sparse sampling and rod–cone mixing. The high number of rod-to-OFF cone-bipolar contacts is emphasized; previously suggested rod-to-ON cone-bipolar contacts were not confirmed. The outer retina is offered as a tractable model of conserved nanometer-scale motifs.
summaries.advanced: This symposium review summarizes Behrens et al. (2016) more than reporting a new reconstruction. Putative synapses are inferred without synaptic labels. Functional significance of rod-to-OFF-CBC contacts is contested in cited physiology (e.g. Protti et al. 2005). Species is mouse; ‘lessons’ should not be assumed to transfer to primate fovea.

plain_language_summary: Rod and cone pathways in the eye were thought to meet later in the circuit. This review of a 3D electron-microscope map of mouse outer retina finds they already mix at the first synapse, with several exceptions to the textbook wiring.

ocar.opportunity: Petascale serial-section EM stacks may need huge numbers of template matches to align 2D tiles into 3D; even a small false-match rate would break neurite continuity.
ocar.challenge: Normalized cross-correlation on raw or bandpass-filtered patches still yields false matches when sections are deformed, damaged, or missing, and rejecting suspects also discards true matches.
ocar.action: Buniatyan, Macrina, Ih, Zung, and Seung, on arXiv (2017), preprocess template and source patches with siamese convolutional networks trained to enlarge the NCC gap between true and false matches, tested on serial-section brain EM.
ocar.resolution: Relative to a tuned bandpass baseline, the networks reduce false matches. For adjacent sections with 224-pixel templates, rejecting matches with r_delta below 0.05 removed every error while dropping 0.12% of true matches versus 0.40% for bandpass (about 3.5× more efficient). On a harder across-section 160-pixel task, 0.1% error needed <1% true-match rejection versus 20% for bandpass.
ocar.future_work: The authors want tests of generalization across EM datasets and possible transfer to the segmentation network that follows alignment. Failure modes include templates that lack the keypoints the net has learned (e.g. cell-body interiors).

summaries.beginner: Stitching electron-microscope slices into a 3D brain volume depends on matching image patches. A neural net that pre-cleans those patches makes the classic matching method much less error-prone.
summaries.intermediate: Buniatyan, Macrina, Ih, Zung, and Seung (arXiv, 2017) wrap normalized cross-correlation with siamese convnets trained so true matches score higher than false ones, using serial-section brain EM patches. Supervision is weak: a true match exists somewhere in the source, but its location is not given. Versus a parameter-tuned bandpass filter, false matches fall, and NCC scores become easier to threshold. For adjacent 224-pixel templates, an r_delta cutoff of 0.05 eliminated all tested errors at 0.12% true-match loss (0.40% for bandpass). The method is motivated by alignment workloads that could reach on the order of 100 million matches for a teravoxel volume.
summaries.advanced: Results are on the authors’ EM patch set, not a public leaderboard. The 100-million-match figure is an order-of-magnitude motivation, not a measured runtime. Generalization across datasets is proposed, not shown. The convnet can fail on templates without learned keypoints; raw images can still help on corner-like edges. This is an arXiv CS.CV preprint.

plain_language_summary: Stitching electron-microscope slices into a 3D brain volume depends on matching image patches. A neural net that pre-cleans those patches makes the classic matching method much less error-prone.

ocar.opportunity: Graph Fourier methods based on the Laplacian give global embeddings, but an analyst often wants organization inside a chosen subgraph without throwing away the rest of the network.
ocar.challenge: Ordinary Laplacian eigenvectors are not concentrated on an arbitrary node set, so they mix local and global structure in a way that is hard to steer.
ocar.action: Van De Ville, Demesmaeker, and Preti, in SPIE Optical Engineering + Applications (2017), apply graph Slepians—band-limited signals with maximal energy in a subgraph—to the structural C. elegans connectome and propose a visualization of subgraph organization balanced against global topology.
ocar.resolution: Selecting sensory or motor neurons and varying bandwidth revealed embeddings that reorganize lobes (e.g. ventral/neck versus left/right) while remaining consistent as bandwidth increases. Concentration-based and modified-embedded-distance Slepian designs spanned similar subspaces; the latter is preferred when eigenvalues are used as frequencies.
ocar.future_work: Suggested extensions include graph uncertainty principles, resampling, hierarchical subgraph refinement, and directed graphs. Matlab code is released.

summaries.beginner: Network maps can be viewed through a mathematical lens that zooms in on one group of cells while still remembering the whole worm. The authors illustrate that trick on the C. elegans wiring diagram.
summaries.intermediate: Van De Ville, Demesmaeker, and Preti (SPIE, 2017) illustrate graph Slepians on the C. elegans structural connectome. Slepians are band-limited graph signals concentrated on a chosen subgraph, used here to visualize that subgraph’s organization without ignoring global structure. Demonstrations on sensory and motor neuron sets show embeddings that change with bandwidth but keep a stable large-scale layout. Two design criteria (energy concentration versus modified embedded distance) give similar subspaces; eigenvalues of the latter can serve as frequencies for filtering. Code is provided.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods illustration on one worm connectome, not a biological discovery paper. The graph-bandwidth product K = N_W N_S / N is compared to summed concentrations and is not identical on irregular domains. ‘Optical Engineering + Applications’ is the SPIE meeting venue; an arXiv version exists. No claim is made that Slepians recover known cell classes better than standard spectral clustering.

plain_language_summary: Network maps can be viewed through a mathematical lens that zooms in on one group of cells while still remembering the whole worm. The authors illustrate that trick on the C. elegans wiring diagram.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain connectomes do not isolate how activity is transmitted between two nodes. An engineered two-node cortical culture with a long axon tract would be a controllable ‘connectome unit.’
ocar.challenge: Massive interconnectivity in vivo, and short internodal distances in prior patterned cultures, make it hard to study multichannel transmission without the network collapsing into a uniform sheet.
ocar.action: Chen, Wolf, and Smith, in Journal of Neural Engineering (2017), use axon stretch growth to build paired cortical nodes linked by tracts up to 1 cm, then combine optogenetic stimulation with multi-electrode-array recording.
ocar.resolution: Stimulus representations included direct, synaptic, and multiplexed responses that grew more complex with distance and collapsed at higher stimulation frequencies. Glutamatergic blockade revealed a hierarchy of pathways, some initially latent. Adding stimulus channels had divergent local versus distant effects, and ensembles generally beat single cells at discriminating input patterns. Mean conduction velocity across engineered axons is given as 0.26 m/s.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the preparation as a model for neural-code studies and multichannel stimulation therapies; in vivo translation is not demonstrated.

summaries.beginner: Instead of mapping a whole brain, this team grows two clumps of cortex linked by a long bundle of axons. They then watch how patterns of activity change as they travel from one clump to the other.
summaries.intermediate: Chen, Wolf, and Smith (Journal of Neural Engineering, 2017) engineer a two-node cortico-cortical culture with stretch-grown axon tracts up to 1 cm—an order of magnitude longer than prior modular cultures—and record with MEAs under optical stimulation. Responses include direct, synaptic, and multiplexed components, simplify at high stimulation rates, and expose latent internodal pathways under glutamate-receptor blockade. Ensemble decoding outperformed single cells. Mean conduction velocity is reported as 0.26 m/s and is described as likely an underestimate. The work is framed as an isolated connectome unit for studying the neural code and stimulation therapies.
summaries.advanced: This is an in vitro tissue-engineering study, not an EM connectome. Conduction velocity 0.26 m/s is a mean that omits synaptic delays in the calculation, as the authors note. ‘Hierarchy of latent circuits’ is pharmacological, not anatomical proofreading. Clinical stimulation guidance is speculative. The PDF is an NIH author manuscript.

plain_language_summary: Instead of mapping a whole brain, this team grows two clumps of cortex linked by a long bundle of axons. They then watch how patterns of activity change as they travel from one clump to the other.

ocar.opportunity: A complete synaptic-resolution mushroom-body connectome lets statistical network models be tested on a biologically labeled directed graph rather than on MRI-scale matrices.
ocar.challenge: A four-type wiring diagram invites a stochastic block model, but latent structure may be richer than four discrete blocks.
ocar.action: Priebe, Park, Tang, Athreya, Lyzinski, Vogelstein, Qin, Cocanougher, Eichler, Zlatic, and Cardona, on arXiv (2017), embed the larval Drosophila mushroom-body graph with adjacency spectral embedding and fit a latent structure model via semiparametric Gaussian mixtures.
ocar.resolution: After dropping 13 isolated Kenyon cells, the right-hemisphere MB graph has 213 vertices (100 KC, 21 MBIN, 29 MBON, 63 PN) and 7,536 directed edges, occupying only eight of sixteen type-type blocks. The resulting ‘connectome code’ is presented as capturing latent structure beyond a simple four-block SBM and as reflecting biologically relevant neuronal properties.
ocar.future_work: The introduction frames connectome coding as asking which properties are preserved across individuals and species; those comparative tests are not the empirical content of this extract.

summaries.beginner: Statisticians take the wiring diagram of a larval fruit-fly learning center and draw a compact map of each cell. The map is meant to show hidden structure, not just the four textbook cell classes.
summaries.intermediate: Priebe and colleagues (arXiv, 2017) analyze the complete larval Drosophila mushroom-body connectome (Eichler et al.) from serial-section TEM of the whole nervous system. The right-hemisphere graph, after removing 13 isolated Kenyon cells, has 213 neurons (100 KC, 21 MBIN, 29 MBON, 63 PN) and 7,536 directed edges. They motivate a latent structure model nested between a stochastic block model and a random dot product graph, fitted by Gaussian mixtures in adjacency-spectral-embedding space. The paper’s claim is that this semiparametric ‘connectome code’ recovers latent structure tied to neuronal properties.
summaries.advanced: This is a statistics preprint; biological labels (KC/MBIN/MBON/PN) come from the source connectome. Eight of sixteen blocks are empty by construction of the directed type graph. Model-fit metrics and out-of-sample prediction are not in the selected extract (which moves from introduction into spectral clustering). Isolate removal makes the graph weakly but not strongly connected.

plain_language_summary: Statisticians take the wiring diagram of a larval fruit-fly learning center and draw a compact map of each cell. The map is meant to show hidden structure, not just the four textbook cell classes.

ocar.opportunity: Contextual visual processing depends on long-range excitatory axons, but the functional logic of those inputs onto individual cortical neurons was unknown.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear what parts of visual space synapse onto a cell, how that relates to the cell’s own receptive field, and whether similar features cluster on neighboring spines.
ocar.action: Iacaruso, Gasler, and Hofer, in Nature (2017), map spatial receptive fields of dendritic spines on mouse primary visual cortex neurons with two-photon calcium imaging.
ocar.resolution: Neurons collect functionally diverse inputs from extended visual space. Similar features from the same location cluster on neighboring spines. Putative long-range inputs often land on higher-order branches and are more frequent, and more co-oriented, when the input receptive field is displaced along the axis of the postsynaptic orientation preference. Connectivity thus prefers co-oriented, co-axially aligned partners, a motif suited to elongated-edge amplification.
ocar.future_work: The authors present this as a candidate substrate for contour integration and object grouping; causal tests of that computation are not in this extract.

summaries.beginner: A visual-cortex cell sees a small patch of the world, but its dendrites also listen to other patches. This study maps those listening posts on individual spines and finds they prefer partners that line up with the cell’s favorite orientation.
summaries.intermediate: Iacaruso, Gasler, and Hofer (Nature, 2017) image GCaMP signals in dendritic spines of mouse V1 to map excitatory input receptive fields. Inputs are functionally diverse and spatially extended; similar features from the same location cluster on neighboring spines. Inputs from beyond the somatic receptive field often target higher-order dendrites. Displaced inputs are more common and more co-oriented when offset along the postsynaptic orientation axis, yielding a co-oriented, co-axial connectivity rule. The authors argue this organization can amplify elongated edges.
summaries.advanced: Inputs are inferred from spine calcium, not EM synapses; ‘putative long-range’ is a spatial-RF criterion. Extended Data in the extract repeat main analyses after dropping spines correlated with the parent dendrite (522 spines remaining after removing 26%). Global dendritic contamination is therefore a recognized artifact. The PDF is a Europe PMC author manuscript of the Nature paper.

plain_language_summary: A visual-cortex cell sees a small patch of the world, but its dendrites also listen to other patches. This study maps those listening posts on individual spines and finds they prefer partners that line up with the cell’s favorite orientation.

ocar.opportunity: Serial block-face SEM can collect thousands of aligned images automatically, reducing the distortion and alignment burden of serial-section TEM for hippocampal circuit reconstruction.
ocar.challenge: Large-scale EM reconstruction had been limited by cutting thousands of sections and tracing warped stacks; SB-SEM still faces charging, beam damage, and a segmentation bottleneck.
ocar.action: Kim, Lee, and Lee, in Applied Microscopy (2016), present a technical report of the full reconstruction workflow for synaptic networks in rat hippocampal CA1 using SB-SEM.
ocar.resolution: They report a three-dimensional volume of about 37,000 µm³ with resolution sufficient to identify sub-synaptic structures and trace fine processes, arguing SB-SEM yielded more reliable stacks than ssTEM and sped reconstruction by cutting alignment work. They note tiled imaging can enlarge the field.
ocar.future_work: Electrical charging of non-conductive resin remains a caveat, potentially mitigated by conductive resins. Segmentation, not acquisition, is identified as the remaining bottleneck. The authors intend the method for mapping impaired synapses in neurodegenerative disease.

summaries.beginner: This methods report shows how to reconstruct synapses in a piece of rat hippocampus by shaving the sample inside a scanning electron microscope. The pictures come out already aligned, which saves a lot of stitching work.
summaries.intermediate: Kim, Sang-Hoon Lee, and Kea-Joo Lee (Applied Microscopy, 2016) describe serial block-face SEM reconstruction of synaptic networks in rat CA1. They report a volume of about 37,000 µm³ acquired automatically and say SB-SEM reduced alignment and distortion relative to serial-section TEM. The discussion flags charging and beam damage as limits on lateral resolution and points to conductive resins. Segmentation is called the major remaining bottleneck. The stated aim is connectomic mapping and eventual study of synaptic disease.
summaries.advanced: This is a technical report from Korea Brain Research Institute, not a full connectome of CA1. The 37,000 µm³ figure is the authors’ stated volume; completeness of tracing is not quantified in the extract. Disease applications are prospective. Image quality caveats (charging) are first-order, not footnotes.

plain_language_summary: This methods report shows how to reconstruct synapses in a piece of rat hippocampus by shaving the sample inside a scanning electron microscope. The pictures come out already aligned, which saves a lot of stitching work.

ocar.opportunity: Large brain-connectome projects map neurons inside the head, but behavior is produced by a nervous system that innervates the whole body.
ocar.challenge: Except for C. elegans, whole-body synaptic maps do not exist, and scaling optical and EM methods to large animals faces imaging, clearing, and reconstruction barriers.
ocar.action: Lo and Chiang, in Journal of Neuroscience (2016), expand a SfN Presidential Lecture into a viewpoint on whole-body connectomics, emphasizing optical methods and the need to map brain–body interactions in situ.
ocar.resolution: They argue that consciousness-level understanding requires jointly mapping circuitry, activity, and behavior beyond isolated brains, using MRI, light microscopy, and EM at their respective scales. C. elegans’ 302-neuron whole-body map is the explicit exception among current projects.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a program for mapping whole-body connectomes in large animals; the selected extract’s later pages are references, so specific technical prescriptions in the discussion are not captured here.

summaries.beginner: Most connectome projects map only the brain. This lecture-based essay says we also need the nerves of the rest of the body if we want to explain real behavior.
summaries.intermediate: Lo and Chiang (Journal of Neuroscience, 2016) publish a viewpoints article based on a 2016 SfN Presidential Lecture. They note that contemporary large-scale projects target brain neurons, with C. elegans’ 302-neuron whole-body reconstruction as the main exception, and they argue that complex behavior requires mapping interactions between brain and body. The survey emphasizes optical approaches alongside EM and MRI. The article is programmatic rather than a new dataset.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinion/lecture piece. The selected PDF text runs from the introduction into the reference list, so later technological recommendations are not in the extract. ‘Whole-body connectome’ is a scale argument, not a claim that optical methods already deliver synaptic whole-body maps in large animals.

plain_language_summary: Most connectome projects map only the brain. This lecture-based essay says we also need the nerves of the rest of the body if we want to explain real behavior.

ocar.opportunity: If neurons carried unique cell-surface identities, they could select synaptic partners with molecular precision rather than by proximity alone.
ocar.challenge: Surface-molecule repertoires and extracellular interactions have been catalogued, but linking that diversity to the precision of circuit wiring remains difficult.
ocar.action: de Wit and Ghosh, in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2015), as described in the catalog abstract, review cadherin, neurexin, immunoglobulin, and leucine-rich-repeat superfamilies in the specification of connectivity.
ocar.resolution: The abstract concludes that concerted actions of these protein families may critically contribute to neural-circuit assembly, without claiming that any one family is sufficient.
ocar.future_work: How combinatorial surface codes map onto complete connectomes is left as the outstanding problem.

summaries.beginner: Neurons may choose their partners using families of sticky surface proteins. This review discusses several of those protein families and how they might help build precise circuits.
summaries.intermediate: de Wit and Ghosh (Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2015) review how cadherins, neurexins, immunoglobulin-superfamily proteins, and leucine-rich-repeat proteins could confer cell-surface identities that specify synapses. The catalog abstract states that concerted actions of these families may be critical for circuit assembly, while noting that connecting molecular diversity to wiring precision has been challenging. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Yang, Song, Lu, and Lin, Chemical Reviews (2026), on in-cellulo fabrication of supramolecular protein assemblies, not the de Wit and Ghosh synapse-specification review. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Nature Reviews Neuroscience paper is required for the primary literature discussed there.

plain_language_summary: Neurons may choose their partners using families of sticky surface proteins. This review discusses several of those protein families and how they might help build precise circuits.

ocar.opportunity: High-throughput connectomes will outrun manual cell-typing. Combining connectivity, soma location, and synapse spatial distributions in one probabilistic model could recover types automatically.
ocar.challenge: There is no closed-form optimum for parsing neurons into types and motifs; inference is approximate and slows with data size, and monotonic distance–connectivity likelihoods are too simple for some systems.
ocar.action: Jonas and Kording, in eLife (2014; arXiv preprint in the extract), present a nonparametric Bayesian method and apply it to retina, C. elegans, and the 6502 microprocessor.
ocar.resolution: The model recovers known retinal types better than simpler algorithms and supports connectivity prediction. It also finds structure in C. elegans and automatically discovers spatial/connectivity clusters among MOS transistors in a 6502 reconstruction. Combining data types is presented as the key.
ocar.future_work: MCMC does not guarantee a global optimum; runtime is hours at 1,000 neurons; ~70 retinal types cannot all be distinguished from the available cells. Broader likelihoods and faster inference are proposed.

summaries.beginner: Instead of naming cell types by hand, this method lets a statistical model group neurons from their wiring and positions. It works on retina and worm data, and even on the transistors of an old computer chip.
summaries.intermediate: Jonas and Kording (eLife, 2014) introduce a nonparametric Bayesian clustering of connectome data that jointly uses connectivity, cell-body location, and spatial synapse distributions. They report recovery of known retinal neuron types and better connectivity prediction than simpler algorithms, plus structure in C. elegans and in a 6502 microprocessor graph (gate/C1/C2 terminals). The discussion is frank that inference is approximate (MCMC), that 1,000 neurons took several hours, and that the cells on hand cannot statistically resolve all ~70 anatomical retinal types.
summaries.advanced: The supplied PDF is an arXiv preprint (v1 2014) with a later header date; the catalog DOI is the eLife version—treat page-level details as preprint. The 6502 example is a provocative analogy, not neural tissue. Distance-dependent likelihoods are assumed monotonic. Type discovery is unsupervised relative to some labels but evaluated against known anatomy where available.

plain_language_summary: Instead of naming cell types by hand, this method lets a statistical model group neurons from their wiring and positions. It works on retina and worm data, and even on the transistors of an old computer chip.

ocar.opportunity: Directed connectomes are often summarized by motif counts, clustering coefficients, and transitivity, which are not independent statistics.
ocar.challenge: Node-level ‘who participates in which subgraph’ (motif-role fingerprints) had not been shown to convert cleanly between functional (partial) and structural (induced) counts, nor to generate those global metrics.
ocar.action: McDonnell, Yaveroğlu, Schmerl, Iannella, and Ward, in PLoS ONE (2014), derive matrix conversions among functional and structural motif-role fingerprints, motif fingerprints, and global subgraph counts, and illustrate them on C. elegans chemical-synapse graphs.
ocar.resolution: A vector of functional motif-role fingerprints from any directed adjacency matrix maps invertibly to structural fingerprints, so the two descriptions are equivalent. The same logic extends to role-free fingerprints and standard motif totals. Motif-role fingerprints are shown to underlie directed clustering coefficients and transitivities, suggesting new subtypes. Matlab code is provided.
ocar.future_work: Proposed uses include centrality on synaptic networks, anomaly detection, and finding similar nodes or graphs; those applications are not benchmarked as a connectome biology result in the extract.

summaries.beginner: When scientists count little wiring triangles in a brain graph, they are really counting how each cell sits inside those triangles. This math paper shows those cell-level counts are the building blocks of several popular network scores.
summaries.intermediate: McDonnell et al. (PLoS ONE, 2014) define motif-role fingerprints—per-node counts of participation in directed subgraphs—and prove that functional (partial-subgraph) fingerprints convert to structural (induced-subgraph) fingerprints by an invertible matrix. Analogous results hold without roles and for global motif counts. They emphasize that directed clustering coefficients and transitivities are derived from these fingerprints, and they apply the machinery to public C. elegans hermaphrodite and male chemical-synapse adjacency matrices. Matlab code is included as supporting information.
summaries.advanced: This is a graph-theory methods paper; biological interpretation of C. elegans motifs is not the main result. ‘Functional’ versus ‘structural’ here means partial versus induced subgraphs, not physiology versus anatomy. New clustering-coefficient subtypes are proposed from the algebra, not validated as superior biomarkers.

plain_language_summary: When scientists count little wiring triangles in a brain graph, they are really counting how each cell sits inside those triangles. This math paper shows those cell-level counts are the building blocks of several popular network scores.

ocar.opportunity: Standard graph metrics ignore two neural facts: information has a preferred input–interneuron–output polarity, and computation often uses recurrent high-level paths rather than shortest paths.
ocar.challenge: Small-world rewiring improves some mixing measures while harming others, so it is unclear whether real neural graphs avoid that trade-off.
ocar.action: Lin, Chang, Hsiao, and Lo, in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2014), quantify ‘vertical’ (specific input to specific output) and ‘horizontal’ (one input shared across outputs) high-level propagation in the C. elegans somatic nervous system and a partial Drosophila central-complex network, versus classic small-world graphs.
ocar.resolution: Both biological networks show efficient vertical and horizontal propagation. Small-world graphs trade the two: higher rewiring probability helps horizontal sharing but hurts vertical routing. Reassigning or reversing I/O nodes degrades efficiency even when architecture is unchanged. Direct (level 0) and one-hop (level 1) channel patterns differ, consistent with distinct functions.
ocar.future_work: The discussion links pathway counts to behaviors (head withdrawal versus oxygen-modulated locomotion) as illustrations, not as new causal experiments.

summaries.beginner: Brain networks have an in door, a middle, and an out door. Measuring how signals travel along those directions, not just along shortest shortcuts, shows worm and fly circuits mix and route information more efficiently than simple small-world models.
summaries.intermediate: Lin, Chang, Hsiao, and Lo (Frontiers in Neuroinformatics, 2014) analyze the C. elegans somatic nervous system and a partial Drosophila central-complex network with polarity-aware, high-level pathway counts. Vertical propagation tracks specific input–output pairs; horizontal propagation tracks sharing of one input across outputs. Both real networks are efficient in both directions, whereas Watts–Strogatz rewiring improves horizontal efficiency at the expense of vertical efficiency. Swapping or randomizing input/output labels reduces performance. Direct versus indirect channel matrices suggest different functional regimes.
summaries.advanced: ‘Efficiency’ is a graph-path construct, not measured spike transmission. The Drosophila network is partial (central complex). Error bars on reassignment plots are from 100 realizations. Behavioral anecdotes (OLQ/IL1–RMD versus AQR/PQR–locomotion) are literature links, not new physiology. Polarity labels are annotations, so they are part of the result rather than a purely topological invariant.

plain_language_summary: Brain networks have an in door, a middle, and an out door. Measuring how signals travel along those directions, not just along shortest shortcuts, shows worm and fly circuits mix and route information more efficiently than simple small-world models.

ocar.opportunity: The AII amacrine cell is the textbook hub from rods into cone pathways; a full connectome can test whether it is a simple relay or a multifunctional network node.
ocar.challenge: Physiology and sparse TEM never catalogued its full partner set, and mouse versus rabbit geometry may change apparent synaptic variance.
ocar.action: Marc, Anderson, Jones, Sigulinsky, and Lauritzen, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2014), analyze AII cells in the rabbit retinal connectome, including complete synaptic counts for five AIIs.
ocar.resolution: AII cells contact at least 28 cell classes, including every bipolar class. Besides distributing rod signals, they are implicated in photopic OFF feedback/feedforward, ON–OFF crossover, and cone-pathway inhibition that may switch rod versus cone vision. Sampling is normalized to encounter rates, targeting appears specific and errorless, and partner cohorts are distinguished by synaptic or coupling weights. Homologs in non-mammals are proposed as glycinergic photopic crossover cells, with mammalian rod bipolar expansion as the evolutionary add-on.
ocar.future_work: A complete physiological model still does not fall out of the anatomy; mouse–rabbit differences in span caution against transferring coefficients of variation across species.

summaries.beginner: A famous retinal cell that helps you see in dim light turns out to talk to at least 28 kinds of partners. Far from a simple relay, it sits at the center of several rod and cone networks.
summaries.intermediate: Marc and colleagues (Frontiers in Neural Circuits, 2014) use the rabbit RC1 connectome to re-examine AII amacrine cells. AIIs contact at least 28 classes, including every bipolar class, via class-specific rules (e.g. postsynaptic to rod bipolars, coupled to most ON cone bipolars, mixed with OFF cone bipolars). Complete counts from five AIIs indicate encounter-normalized sampling, apparently errorless qualitative targeting, and strong weight differentiation. The cell is framed as a dense hub for scotopic distribution plus photopic crossover and switching. An evolutionary sketch posits non-mammalian glycinergic homologs plus later expansion of pure rod bipolars.
summaries.advanced: ‘Most complex interaction repertoire of any known vertebrate neuron’ is an authorship claim. ‘Errorless’ targeting is reported for this volume and cell sample. Mouse CV comparisons (Tsukamoto and Omi) are attributed to smaller mouse spans (~10 μm versus rabbit AII spans of 70 μm or more). TH1 cells are reidentified as glutamatergic, not dual GABAergic/dopaminergic, in this rabbit profiling. Catalog organism tags include mouse; the paper is rabbit RC1.

plain_language_summary: A famous retinal cell that helps you see in dim light turns out to talk to at least 28 kinds of partners. Far from a simple relay, it sits at the center of several rod and cone networks.

ocar.opportunity: The hippocampal mossy-fiber bouton is among the largest synapses in the brain, but its postnatal assembly is hard to reconstruct with serial-section TEM.
ocar.challenge: Standard EM could not quickly capture aligned volumes spanning developing boutons, thorny excrescences, and filopodia together.
ocar.action: Wilke, Antonios, Bushong, Badkoobehi, Malek, Hwang, Terada, Ellisman, and Ghosh, in Journal of Neuroscience (2013), use serial block-face EM to reconstruct mouse mossy-fiber connectivity across postnatal development.
ocar.resolution: Mossy-fiber axons first make bouton-like specializations on dendritic shafts; dendritic protrusions largely arise independently of those contacts; complexity of both sides jumps after bouton–CA3 protrusion association. A transient filopodial exploration period is followed by refinement. Between P14 and adult, many small contacts appear to become fewer, larger synaptic sites. Occasional multi-bouton innervation of one thorny spine and dual-dendrite targeting at P14 were not seen in adult.
ocar.future_work: Whether small sites compete or merge, and how these structural stages map onto detonator-synapse physiology, remains open. The paper presents SBEM as a general developmental-circuit tool.

summaries.beginner: The giant mossy-fiber synapse in hippocampus is built in stages after birth. Volume electron microscopy shows early contacts on the dendritic shaft, a messy exploratory phase, then a cleaned-up adult structure.
summaries.intermediate: Wilke et al. (Journal of Neuroscience, 2013) apply SBEM to mouse mossy-fiber–CA3 synapses at postnatal ages including P7, P14, and adult. Volume reconstructions indicate initial shaft boutons, largely independent emergence of dendritic protrusions, then a sharp rise in pre- and postsynaptic complexity once boutons associate with CA3 thorny excrescences, followed by filopodial exploration and later refinement. Background anatomy cited includes 10–15 mossy terminals per granule cell, ~50 dentate inputs per CA3 neuron, and up to 37 release sites per bouton. P14 still shows multi-bouton spines and dual-dendrite contacts absent in adult.
summaries.advanced: Developmental claims are from SBEM volumes at sampled ages, not longitudinal imaging of the same synapses. The 10–15, ~50, and 37 figures are cited from prior literature (Amaral, Acsády, Chicurel and Harris), not new counts in the extract. Competitive versus merger models of contact refinement are offered as alternatives. Functional ‘detonator’ language is background, not measured here.

plain_language_summary: The giant mossy-fiber synapse in hippocampus is built in stages after birth. Volume electron microscopy shows early contacts on the dendritic shaft, a messy exploratory phase, then a cleaned-up adult structure.

ocar.opportunity: If ON and OFF inner plexiform layers were strictly segregated, ON cone bipolar axons should be silent in the OFF stratum. A dense retinal connectome can test that textbook split.
ocar.challenge: Sparse EM and light microscopy could miss noncanonical axonal ribbons and the joint-distribution statistics of sparse targets.
ocar.action: Lauritzen, Anderson, Jones, Watt, Mohammed, Hoang, and Marc, in Journal of Comparative Neurology (2013), use automated TEM, molecular tagging, and tracing of about 400 bipolar cells in rabbit connectome RC1.
ocar.resolution: The ON/OFF IPL split is not structurally absolute. Axonal ribbons occur in 36% of ON cone bipolar cells throughout the OFF IPL, targeting GABAergic and glycinergic amacrine cells and ganglion cells, and creating motifs for ON–OFF amacrine generation and OFF-to-ON crossover inhibition. Incidence is a joint distribution of axon frequency and target trajectories. Müller sheaths part at contact sites.
ocar.future_work: Molecular mechanisms of targeting and why some ON cells invade the OFF layer remain open; the authors reframe the question toward mixed ON–OFF strata rather than a purified OFF layer.

summaries.beginner: Textbooks split the inner retina into ON and OFF layers. A rabbit connectome shows ON bipolar axons still making synapses in the so-called OFF layer, creating extra mixing and crossover circuits.
summaries.intermediate: Lauritzen et al. (Journal of Comparative Neurology, 2013) analyze rabbit retinal connectome RC1. Automated TEM, molecular tags, and reconstruction of ≈400 bipolar cells show axonal ribbons in 36% of ON cone bipolars throughout the OFF inner plexiform layer. Targets include GABA- and glycine-positive amacrine cells and ganglion cells, supporting new ON–OFF amacrine architectures and OFF-to-ON crossover inhibition, plus polarity-appropriate drive of some bistratified ganglion cells. Drive incidence is treated as a joint distribution of source axons and sparse target paths, especially given ON bipolar coupling.
summaries.advanced: The catalog organism tag is mouse; the paper is rabbit RC1. 36% is the stated fraction of ON cone bipolars with axonal ribbons, not a synapse-level error rate. Conflict-of-interest: Marc is a principal of Signature Immunologics, which made some reagents. Evolutionary argument (OFF layer never purified in vertebrates) is interpretive. PDF is an NIH author manuscript.

plain_language_summary: Textbooks split the inner retina into ON and OFF layers. A rabbit connectome shows ON bipolar axons still making synapses in the so-called OFF layer, creating extra mixing and crossover circuits.

ocar.opportunity: Hubel and Wiesel’s functional architecture still organizes how cortical connectivity is discussed: topography, cell type, and function as separate specificities.
ocar.challenge: Thalamic input to simple cells was verified, but intracortical functional specificity—whether neurons connect by what they encode, not only by where they sit—was only becoming experimentally tractable.
ocar.action: Reid, in Neuron (2012), revisits the 1962 Hubel and Wiesel paper and subsequent slice and in vivo work, including Peters’ rule as a null model of non-specific connectivity.
ocar.resolution: Orientation columns exemplify topographic specificity. Fine-scale functional specificity of thalamic input to simple cells was confirmed in the 1990s. A simplifying assumption that neurons of a class are equivalent, with synapses reflecting availability (Peters’ rule), is contrasted with emerging evidence for more specific intracortical wiring. Cell-type architecture from slices is reviewed as necessary but not sufficient.
ocar.future_work: The essay points to new techniques as the way to settle intracortical functional specificity; it is not itself a connectomic reconstruction.

summaries.beginner: A classic 1962 vision paper taught us that cortex is organized in columns. This essay explains how that idea splits into ‘where a cell sits,’ ‘what type it is,’ and ‘what it encodes,’ and why the last piece was still the hardest to map in 2012.
summaries.intermediate: Reid (Neuron, 2012) commemorates Hubel and Wiesel (1962), extracting topographic specificity (e.g. orientation columns), cell-type specificity, and functional specificity as distinct determinants of cortical connectivity. Thalamic models of simple-cell input are described as verified in the 1990s, while intracortical functional specificity remained the open, harder problem. Slice work on stereotyped connections (e.g. chandelier cells onto axon initial segments) is summarized, and Peters’ rule is presented as the canonical non-specific alternative. The piece is a conceptual review, not new data.
summaries.advanced: This is a historical/theoretical Neuron article. Peters’ rule is discussed as a corollary of class-equivalence, not refuted with a new dataset here. ‘Only now becoming tractable’ is a 2012 claim about methods (two-photon, EM). The PDF is an NIH author manuscript; the citation to Lee and Reid 2011 is the companion Current Opinion review in this shard.

plain_language_summary: A classic 1962 vision paper taught us that cortex is organized in columns. This essay explains how that idea splits into ‘where a cell sits,’ ‘what type it is,’ and ‘what it encodes,’ and why the last piece was still the hardest to map in 2012.

ocar.opportunity: Identified-neuron circuits in larval zebrafish can be turned into a graph that is detailed enough to compare with random and small-world nulls and to simulate lesions.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear which graph statistics a vertebrate sensorimotor pathway would show, and whether removing a few known command-like cells would change path structure as behavior predicts.
ocar.action: Stobb, Peterson, Mazzag, and Gahtan, in PLoS ONE (2012), build a graph of the posterior lateral line sensorimotor pathway with 2,616 neurons and 167,114 synapses set stochastically from literature rules, then compare 100 instantiations of several null graphs and lesion three hindbrain cells including the Mauthner neuron.
ocar.resolution: Density is 2.45% of possible connections. Degree variation exceeds less biological nulls. High clustering and short path length imply small-world structure; the graph is not scale-free. The Mauthner-including lesion reduced short sensory-to-motor paths, analogous to the behavioral lesion. The model is offered as an expandable database for the zebrafish connectome.
ocar.future_work: Supporting models with dedicated versus distributed inter-compartment wiring still matched degree and small-world measures despite changing >20% of connections, so those global stats are not unique fingerprints of the anatomical rule set.

summaries.beginner: Researchers built a detailed wiring model of how a larval zebrafish feels water flow and turns its body. The model looks small-world, and cutting out three famous command cells shortens the easy paths from sensors to muscles.
summaries.intermediate: Stobb, Peterson, Mazzag, and Gahtan (PLoS ONE, 2012) present a graph-theoretical model of the zebrafish posterior lateral line pathway: 2,616 neurons and 167,114 synapses, with types and stochastic connections taken from the literature. Connection density is 2.45%. Compared with 100 instantiations each of small-world, random, and structured-random graphs of the same size, the zebrafish graph has broader degree variation, high clustering, short mean path length, and is not scale-free. Lesioning three model hindbrain neurons including Mauthner reduced short sensorimotor paths, matching known behavior.
summaries.advanced: This is a literature-based generative model, not an EM reconstruction. Counts of cells (e.g. interneurons from zfin.org atlases) are estimates. Dedicated and distributed variants in the supplement change >20% of inter-compartment edges yet keep similar degree and small-world scores, so those metrics are coarse. Expandability is a design claim.

plain_language_summary: Researchers built a detailed wiring model of how a larval zebrafish feels water flow and turns its body. The model looks small-world, and cutting out three famous command cells shortens the easy paths from sensors to muscles.

ocar.opportunity: High-resolution EM can stream petascale 2D tiles continuously; visualization needs a 3D multi-resolution view without waiting to build a full octree of the entire acquisition.
ocar.challenge: Prior volume renderers either coupled hierarchy construction to acquisition or made sample access time grow with hierarchy size, and they did not treat missing data as a first-class state.
ocar.action: Hadwiger, Beyer, Jeong, and Pfister, in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2012), as described in the catalog abstract, present a visualization-driven virtual-memory architecture for streaming EM volumes.
ocar.resolution: The abstract states that the system decouples multi-resolution construction from acquisition and decouples ray-casting sample access from hierarchy size, builds 3D blocks from 2D tiles only when ray-casting requests them, and handles missing data as cache misses. Effectiveness is illustrated on real neuroscience EM.
ocar.future_work: How the architecture compares on later petascale pipelines is outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can pour out more pictures than a computer can store as a finished 3D pyramid. This paper describes a viewer that builds only the pieces of the volume you are actually looking at.
summaries.intermediate: Hadwiger, Beyer, Jeong, and Pfister (IEEE TVCG, 2012) describe, per the catalog abstract, the first volume visualization system claimed to scale to petascale EM streams. A multi-resolution virtual memory accepts a constant stream of 2D tiles, does not precompute an octree, and constructs 3D blocks on demand when ray-casting hits missing data. The design is visualization-driven: most computation is restricted to visible data. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Wan et al., BMC Bioinformatics (2017), on FluoRender many-channel fluorescence visualization, not the Hadwiger et al. EM virtual-memory system. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the IEEE TVCG paper is required for benchmarks versus prior systems.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can pour out more pictures than a computer can store as a finished 3D pyramid. This paper describes a viewer that builds only the pieces of the volume you are actually looking at.

ocar.opportunity: A wiring diagram cannot predict behavior because neuromodulation superimposes a chemical map on synapses. A brain-wide genetic reporter of modulator receptor activation would locate that map in identified cells.
ocar.challenge: Voltammetry and microdialysis are limited in Drosophila and do not identify postsynaptic targets of released modulators.
ocar.action: Inagaki, Ben-Tabou de-Leon, Wong, Jagadish, Ishimoto, Barnea, Kitamoto, Axel, and Anderson, in Cell (2012), introduce TANGO-mapping of dopamine signaling and combine it with genetic perturbations of hunger-dependent sugar sensitivity.
ocar.resolution: Hunger enhances behavioral sensitivity to sugar at least in part via dopamine onto primary gustatory receptor neurons, increasing sugar-evoked calcium influx. DopR-Tango reports starvation-induced dopamine onto GRNs but not, under the same conditions, onto mushroom body or antennal lobe despite L-dopa feeding activating those sites. DopEcR mutation or GRN knockdown blocks the starvation effect at 6 h but not at 24 h of deprivation.
ocar.future_work: The method is offered for other neuromodulators and organisms. Later-stage starvation appears to recruit additional mechanisms beyond DopEcR in GRNs.

summaries.beginner: A connectome list of synapses cannot tell you how a hungry fly will act, because chemicals such as dopamine retune the circuit. This paper introduces a genetic map of where dopamine lands and shows it turns up sugar sensors when the fly is hungry.
summaries.intermediate: Inagaki et al. (Cell, 2012) introduce TANGO-mapping to report sites of neuromodulation brain-wide in Drosophila. Applied to dopamine, the method plus genetics shows hunger increases sugar-evoked calcium in primary gustatory neurons via dopamine release onto those cells, contributing to enhanced PER sugar sensitivity. Starvation raised DopR-Tango in GRNs but not mushroom body or antennal lobe, even though L-dopa feeding could activate the latter. Knockdown or mutation of DopEcR in sugar GRNs removed the 6-hour starvation effect but not the 24-hour effect, implying additional later mechanisms.
summaries.advanced: TANGO is a transcriptional reporter, not a millisecond release assay; spatial resolution is cell class, not synapse. The 6 h versus 24 h split is an important caveat for claiming a single dopaminergic mechanism. The paper’s opening claim that behavior cannot be predicted from a connectome is a framing thesis, not a failed prediction on a specific EM graph. PDF is an NIH author manuscript; title retains the published ‘Appeptite’ spelling.

plain_language_summary: A connectome list of synapses cannot tell you how a hungry fly will act, because chemicals such as dopamine retune the circuit. This paper introduces a genetic map of where dopamine lands and shows it turns up sugar sensors when the fly is hungry.

ocar.opportunity: Explaining computation and its metabolic cost requires annotated graphs of synapses and of vessels. New histology and imaging were beginning to make both graphs realistic.
ocar.challenge: Neuronal and vascular architectures constrain algorithms and nutrient delivery; assembling those graphs needs 3D hardware plus software and machine learning spanning tens of nanometers to micrometers.
ocar.action: Kleinfeld, Bharioke, Blinder, Bock, Briggman, Chklovskii, Denk, Helmstaedter, Kaufhold, Lee, Meyer, Micheva, Oberlaender, Prohaska, Reid, Smith, Takemura, Tsai, and Sakmann, in Journal of Neuroscience (2011), summarize a mini-symposium on large-scale automated histology for connectomes and angiomes.
ocar.resolution: They frame analysis at tens of nanometers as yielding connections between identified neurons, and micrometer-scale analysis as yielding probabilistic neuronal connection rules plus exact vascular connectivity. Vascular graphs are presented as a comparatively simple undirected connectome sufficient, with length/radius annotations, to calculate cortical flow.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a 2011 state-of-the-art survey; the selected extract’s latter portion is references, so individual talk results should be read in the cited primary papers.

summaries.beginner: To understand how brains compute and how they are fueled, we need maps of both synapses and blood vessels. This 2011 survey sketches the microscopes and software then being built to draw those maps automatically.
summaries.intermediate: Kleinfeld and a large multi-lab author list (Journal of Neuroscience, 2011) write a mini-symposium review on automated histology for neuronal connectomes and vascular graphs. They argue that nanometer-scale analysis identifies synapses between reconstructed neurons, whereas micrometer-scale analysis gives probabilistic wiring rules and exact vascular connectivity. The vascular ‘angiome’ is introduced as an annotated graph whose connectivity and vessel geometry suffice to compute flow. The article is a field snapshot, not a single new volume.
summaries.advanced: This is a multi-author SfN mini-symposium write-up. Claims are programmatic and cite then-current methods (SBEM, array tomography, all-optical histology, etc.) rather than a unified dataset. The selected PDF text does not include a quantitative comparison table; later pages are references. Treat lab-specific numbers as belonging to the cited papers.

plain_language_summary: To understand how brains compute and how they are fueled, we need maps of both synapses and blood vessels. This 2011 survey sketches the microscopes and software then being built to draw those maps automatically.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-mouse-brain light microscopy at sub-micrometer resolution sits between diffusion MRI and serial EM, but the resulting multiscale volumes are hard even to view, let alone quantify as connectivity.
ocar.challenge: KESM datasets span subcellular to organ scales (Golgi circuits, Nissl somata, India-ink vessels), so visualization and analysis needed a dedicated informatics layer.
ocar.action: Chung, Sung, Mayerich, Kwon, Miller, Huffman, Keyser, Abbott, and Choe, in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2011), describe the Knife-Edge Scanning Microscope Brain Atlas (KESMBA), a web framework for those volumes.
ocar.resolution: KESMBA is presented as an efficient browser for multiscale KESM data, filling a resolution/volume gap relevant to connectomics. The authors outline needed next steps: all three standard section planes, overlay and editing of automated reconstructions, uncertainty visualization, and tools to specify axon–dendrite connectivity.
ocar.future_work: Without synapse-level links, Golgi KESM remains a morphology atlas rather than a connectome; the paper treats that gap as the informatics agenda.

summaries.beginner: A special microscope can photograph an entire mouse brain in fine detail, but the files are huge. This paper describes a web atlas so researchers can zoom from the whole brain down toward cells and vessels.
summaries.intermediate: Chung, Sung, Mayerich, Kwon, Miller, Huffman, Keyser, Abbott, and Choe (Frontiers in Neuroinformatics, 2011) introduce KESMBA, a web-based atlas for Knife-Edge Scanning Microscope whole-mouse-brain datasets stained for Golgi (neurites), Nissl (somata), and India ink (vasculature). They position KESM between large-volume low-resolution MRI and small-volume EM, and argue that visualization is a prerequisite for quantitative connectivity. Future extensions include multi-plane viewing, reconstruction overlays, editing, and manual or parametric synapse/proximity specification.
summaries.advanced: KESM is optical serial cutting, not synaptic-resolution EM; Golgi does not label all cells or synapses. Connectomics relevance is a gap-filling argument. Movie supplements showcase data independently of the web UI. Parameter-constraining remarks for simulations are prospective.

plain_language_summary: A special microscope can photograph an entire mouse brain in fine detail, but the files are huge. This paper describes a web atlas so researchers can zoom from the whole brain down toward cells and vessels.

ocar.opportunity: Wiring diagrams without physiology cannot explain computation. New functional imaging plus large-scale EM finally let structure–function questions be asked in cortex and retina.
ocar.challenge: Topographic and cell-type specificity are comparatively well described; functional specificity—whether connections respect encoded features—is not, and C. elegans shows that a complete graph without rich physiology is not enough.
ocar.action: Lee and Reid, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2011), review how two-photon imaging and EM have begun to relate sensory physiology to synapses in cortical and retinal circuits.
ocar.resolution: They contrast a mosaic, locally specific retina with a more integrative cortex in which excitatory neurons may show functional specificity while inhibitory cells appear more promiscuous. Recent large-scale EM is said to confirm function-based structural predictions in well-understood systems. The Bock et al. cortical EM volume is noted as public (CCDB 8448; Open Connectome Project).
ocar.future_work: Richer EM (more function, biochemical labels, long-range dense staining, volumetric synapse size as a strength proxy) and multi-investigator mining of public volumes are the stated path.

summaries.beginner: Having a wiring diagram is not the same as knowing what the circuit computes. This review explains new ways to match each cell’s sensory responses to its synapses in the eye and in visual cortex.
summaries.intermediate: Lee and Reid (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2011) review structure–function specificity. They distinguish topographic and cell-type specificity from functional specificity and argue the last is the missing piece for information processing. Retina is framed as tiled parallel processors with specific local wiring; cortex as more integrative, with functionally specific excitatory connections and more promiscuous inhibition. Large-scale EM is described as beginning to confirm functional predictions. The Bock dataset is cited as a public resource (CCDB accession 8448).
summaries.advanced: This is a short review; primary measurements live in the cited EM/physiology papers. The C. elegans caveat (graph without physiology) is conceptual. Inhibitory promiscuity versus excitatory specificity is a 2011 synthesis, not a new count. PDF is an NIH author manuscript.

plain_language_summary: Having a wiring diagram is not the same as knowing what the circuit computes. This review explains new ways to match each cell’s sensory responses to its synapses in the eye and in visual cortex.

ocar.opportunity: The human connectome names a highly organized connection matrix, but information flow through that matrix is so complex that a complete synaptic diagram is unlikely soon.
ocar.challenge: Circuit diagrams can be drawn at several scales; completing them at the synaptic level is described as surely impossible, which risks leaving ultrastructure disconnected from macro maps.
ocar.action: DeFelipe, in Science (2010), as described in the catalog abstract, argues for marrying macroscopic and microscopic data into a realistic statistical ‘synaptome.’
ocar.resolution: The abstract offers optimism that statistical models of ultrastructural connectivity, rather than exhaustive synapse-by-synapse completion, could make the synaptome tractable.
ocar.future_work: How such a statistical synaptome would be parameterized and validated is left open in the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Listing every human brain synapse is probably impossible. This essay says we should instead build statistical models of synapses that still connect to larger-scale brain maps.
summaries.intermediate: DeFelipe (Science, 2010) discusses the newly named human connectome and the difficulty of tracing information flow through it. Per the catalog abstract, complete synaptic-level diagrams are treated as unattainable in the near term, yet combining macro- and microscopic measurements might yield a realistic statistical model of ultrastructural connectivity—the synaptome. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Li et al., bioRxiv (2025), on functional fractionation of large-scale networks in the human subcortex, not the DeFelipe Science essay. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the 2010 Science piece is required for the full argument and figures.

plain_language_summary: Listing every human brain synapse is probably impossible. This essay says we should instead build statistical models of synapses that still connect to larger-scale brain maps.

ocar.opportunity: EM volumes of mammalian neuropil can reach tens of terabytes to about a petabyte, so interactive visualization and analysis tools are a prerequisite for circuit reconstruction.
ocar.challenge: Existing viewers and segmenters did not scale to arbitrary sizes, complex 3D neurites, or network retrieval; ATLUM-class devices were already producing about a terabyte per day.
ocar.action: Jeong, Beyer, Hadwiger, Law, Vázquez-Reina, Reid, Lichtman, and Pfister, in IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications (2010), present Ssecrett and NeuroTrace for interactive exploration of large optical and EM datasets.
ocar.resolution: The tools are described as supporting visualization and analysis aimed at reconstructing mammalian circuits. A 1 mm³ sample at 5 nm × 5 nm × 30 nm is about one petabyte of raw data. Related-work discussion contrasts Reconstruct, NeuronJ, Imaris, and Amira as lacking Ssecrett’s combination of scale, 3D complexity, and networked access.
ocar.future_work: Automated EM segmentation methods cited then had not been shown to scale to these sizes; visualization research had mostly addressed gigabyte, not petabyte, volumes.

summaries.beginner: Modern electron microscopes create brain-image files so large that ordinary viewers choke. This paper introduces two tools meant to let scientists browse and analyze those volumes while tracing neurons.
summaries.intermediate: Jeong, Beyer, Hadwiger, Law, Vázquez-Reina, Reid, Lichtman, and Pfister (IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications, 2010) introduce Ssecrett and NeuroTrace for interactive work on large optical and EM neuroscience datasets. They size a 1 mm³ EM volume at 5 nm in-plane and 30 nm section thickness at about one petabyte, with ATLUM-like acquisition near one terabyte per day. Challenges include low-latency access to arbitrary regions and scalable filtering, segmentation, and visualization. Prior tools are judged inadequate for arbitrarily large, complex 3D neurites with networked data access.
summaries.advanced: This is a systems/visualization article; reconstruction accuracy metrics are not the focus of the extract. Petabyte and TB/day figures are order-of-magnitude engineering estimates for stated resolutions. Author list in the PDF includes additional Kitware contributors (e.g. Rusty Blue) relative to the catalog string. NIH author manuscript.

plain_language_summary: Modern electron microscopes create brain-image files so large that ordinary viewers choke. This paper introduces two tools meant to let scientists browse and analyze those volumes while tracing neurons.
